content: Ungulates are mammals characterized by their use of the tips of their toes, which are typically covered by hooves, to support their body weight during movement. These animals belong to several mammalian orders, with six to eight of these orders still existing today. There is ongoing debate among scientists about whether ungulates form a true evolutionary group (cladistic) or are simply grouped together based on similar physical traits (phenetic), as not all ungulates are as closely related as previously thought. Historically, Ungulata was considered a single order, but it has since been divided into several orders, including Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, Tubulidentata, Hyracoidea, Sirenia, and Proboscidea. The term true ungulates refers to members of Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, and Cetacea, distinguishing them from subungulates (paenungulates), which include Proboscidea, Sirenia, Hyracoidea, and Tubulidentata. Examples of modern ungulates include horses, zebras, donkeys, cattle, bison, rhinoceroses, camels, hippopotamuses, goats, pigs, sheep, giraffes, okapis, deer, tapirs, antelopes, and gazelles. The largest groups of ungulates are Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates) and Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates), which together comprise the majority of large land mammals. These groups first appeared during the late Paleocene and early Eocene, approximately 54 million years ago, and rapidly diversified into numerous species across various continents. Although whales and dolphins (Cetacea) lack many of the typical physical traits of ungulates, recent evidence suggests that they evolved from early artiodactyls and are closely related to even-toed ungulates such as cattle and hippopotamuses. This discovery has led to the proposal of a new order, Cetartiodactyla, which combines Artiodactyla and Cetacea to reflect their shared ancestry. However, some scientists argue that Cetacea can simply be recognized as a subgroup within Artiodactyla without the need for a new order. The Paenungulata, which include Hyracoidea, Sirenia, and Proboscidea, are considered distinct from the true ungulates. Tubulidentata (aardvarks) are also thought to be ungulates, and some studies suggest they may be linked to Paenungulata within a group called Pseudoungulata. Genetic evidence indicates that Pseudoungulates are not closely related to artiodactyls and perissodactyls. Instead, their closest relatives are Afrosoricida (a group of small African mammals), and together they form a larger group known as Afrotheria. Fossil evidence reveals additional extinct ungulate groups, such as embrithopods, desmostylians, mesonychids, condylarths, and various South American and Paleogene lineages. Ungulates share several anatomical traits, including reduced canine teeth, bunodont molars (molars with low, rounded cusps), and a specialized ankle bone called the astragalus, which has a short, robust head. Another common feature is the fusion of the radius and ulna in the forelimbs, which prevents rotation of the forelimb. This skeletal structure is considered a homologous trait inherited from a common ancestor, although it does not serve a specific function in modern ungulates. Early ungulates, such as arctocyonids, did not exhibit this fused forelimb structure. Ungulates are thought to have originated as far back as the late Cretaceous period and diversified rapidly during the Eocene. While most ungulates are herbivores, some, such as the extinct Mesonychia and modern whales, are omnivores or predators. Recent molecular and genetic studies have challenged traditional views of ungulate relationships. For example, Perissodactyla and Cetartiodactyla appear to be more closely related to Carnivora (carnivores) and Pholidota (pangolins) than to Pseudoungulata. Pseudoungulata, in turn, are grouped with Afrosoricida within Afrotheria based on DNA evidence, suggesting they are not related to other ungulates. The extinct South American ungulates, which evolved in isolation during the mid to late Paleocene, are classified in a super-order called Meridiungulata. Some researchers believe these animals are unrelated to other ungulates and instead group them with Afrotheria and Xenarthra in a larger supercohort called Atlantogenata. Other extinct ungulates, such as embrithopods and desmostylians, are considered relatives of Paenungulata and members of Afrotheria. The condylarths, once thought to be the ancestors of all ungulates, are now believed to belong to Laurasiatheria, a different evolutionary group. As a result, only Perissodactyla and Artiodactyla are thought to have descended from condylarths, assuming the animals historically grouped as condylarths are even related to one another. These findings suggest that the typical ungulate body plan evolved independently at least three times: in Meridiungulata, Afrotheria, and the true ungulates of Laurasiatheria. However, some scientists remain skeptical of dividing ungulates into so many unrelated clades, citing a lack of morphological evidence to support such divisions.
